The Many-ribbed salamander (Eurycea multiplicata) emerges from its gelatinous egg mass after a relatively brief developmental period; when eggs are incubated at a constant water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the embryo completes its yolk-dependent development and hatches in approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days]. This incubation interval is among the shorter durations recorded for plethodontid salamanders of similar body size, likely reflecting a selective pressure to exploit temporally constrained aquatic habitats in the Ozark and Ouachita highlands. At the moment of eclosion, the newly emerged larva possesses a snout–vent length of roughly 0.95 cm [Lb = roughly 0.95 cm], a dimension that is consistent with the modest egg diameters typical of the genus Eurycea. This small initial size places the neonate at a competitive disadvantage relative to co-occurring larval amphibians, necessitating a rapid onset of exogenous feeding once the yolk sac is resorbed. Field observations indicate that the transition to active filter feeding and buccal grazing occurs within the first few days post-hatching, marking the start of a prolonged larval growth phase during which the animal accumulates the somatic resources required for subsequent metamorphic transformation.

As the aquatic larva progresses through successive Gosner stages, its body undergoes considerable allometric expansion, culminating in an ultimate snout–vent length of 4.2 cm [Li = 4.2 cm] at the completion of metamorphosis, while the total length including the tail can approach 7.8 cm. The corresponding snout–vent length at this critical developmental milestone, the metamorphic climax, has been measured at 3.3 cm  in individuals collected from spring-fed streams in the Boston Mountains of Arkansas. This value, which reflects the larval-juvenile transition, is broadly comparable to the metamorphic SVL reported for other members of the Eurycea bislineata species complex. The allometric shift during metamorphosis involves the resorption of the caudal fin and gill structures, the development of functional lungs, and the keratinisation of the integument, all of which facilitate the transition from an obligately aquatic existence to a semi-terrestrial lifestyle among the moist leaf litter and crevices of the riparian zone. Growth does not cease entirely at metamorphosis, however, as the juvenile continues to accrue body mass throughout the subsequent months.

Sexual maturation in Many-ribbed salamander is attained when individuals have reached a total length of 3.4 cm [Lp = 3.4 cm], a measurement that encompasses the complete body from the snout to the tail tip. This size threshold, which signals the onset of gametogenesis, is supported by gonadal inspection of preserved museum specimens, which consistently reveal the presence of mature oocytes or spermatocytes only in animals exceeding this total length. The age at which this length is achieved is variable and is strongly influenced by the thermal regime of the natal stream; under the cool, stable conditions typical of their groundwater-fed habitats, puberty is often deferred until the second or third year of life. Adult individuals can attain a snout–vent length of 4.2 cm [Li = 4.2 cm], which is among the largest recorded for the Eurycea bislineata complex and represents the upper bound of continuous somatic growth. This decoupling of size and reproductive maturity is a common feature among plethodontid salamanders and is thought to buffer populations against the demographic consequences of unpredictable juvenile survival.

The maximum adult wet body mass reported for Eurycea multiplicata reaches 2.0 grams [Wwi = 2.0 grams] in large, robust females collected during the breeding season. This asymptotic mass likely represents a physiological ceiling imposed by the constraints of the animal's slender, elongated body plan and the limited foraging opportunities afforded by its subterranean and leaf-litter microhabitats. For comparative context, a closely related species, the cave salamander Eurycea lucifuga, attains a similar asymptotic wet weight of approximately 2.6 grams at a larger SVL, suggesting that the scaling relationship between length and mass in Eurycea multiplicata is slightly more slender-bodied. The attainment of this maximum mass is typically observed in individuals that have survived multiple breeding seasons and have accumulated sufficient fat reserves within their tail region, which serves as the primary storage organ. Condition indices derived from the ratio of mass to length are frequently used by field biologists as a proxy for overall health and energetic status in this species, with values declining markedly during the protracted winter dormancy period.

Longevity data for Many-ribbed salamander, derived from mark-recapture studies conducted in the Ozark National Forest and maintained at a constant ambient temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 9.1 years [am = approximately 9.1 years]. This estimate, which is based on the observed persistence of individually marked adults across consecutive field seasons, is broadly concordant with the life spans reported for other spring-dwelling Eurycea species that experience similarly cool and thermally stable environments. A life span approaching a decade is remarkably long for an amphibian of this diminutive size and is thought to be facilitated by a slow metabolic rate, reduced predation pressure in groundwater habitats, and a life-history strategy that prioritises adult survival over high fecundity. The relatively delayed senescence observed in this species stands in contrast to the more rapid life cycles of many pond-breeding ambystomatid salamanders, which rarely exceed four years in the wild. Continued monitoring of tagged populations will be essential to determine whether this maximum longevity is consistently expressed across the species' broader geographic range.
